study_identification.title: Revealing Individual Neuroanatomical Heterogeneity in Alzheimer Disease Using Neuroanatomical Normative Modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: To characterize individual differences and outliers in cortical thickness in patients with Alzheimer disease (AD), people with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and controls using neuroanatomical normative modeling. The study assessed relationships between cortical thickness heterogeneity and cognitive function, β-amyloid, phosphorylated-tau, and ApoE genotype, and examined whether cortical thickness heterogeneity predicted conversion from MCI to AD.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) with site-specific random effects to account for intersite variation. The model adaptively pools parameter estimates across 60 sites in the reference dataset via shared priors over regression parameters, allowing sites to borrow strength from one another in a fully Bayesian framework. For application to ADNI (62 sites), an adapted transfer learning approach was used: the reference normative model parameters were recalibrated using 70% of healthy controls per ADNI site (stratified across sites and gender). This transfer learning ensured stable estimates given that many ADNI scan sites have small sample sizes. The remaining 30% of healthy controls plus MCI and AD patients were used for heterogeneity assessment.
site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper provides extensive detail on the hierarchical Bayesian regression approach for handling site effects. It describes the adaptive pooling mechanism, the Bayesian framework, and the specific transfer learning strategy used to adapt the reference model to ADNI sites. The rationale for using 70% of controls for calibration is also explained (to ensure stable estimates given small sample sizes at individual ADNI sites).
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: A hierarchical Bayesian regression model was trained on multisite data to generate normative models per region using the covariates age and sex. This was based on the population variation in the reference data set (training data), which adaptively pools parameter estimates across sites via a shared prior over regression parameters across sites. This simultaneously accounts for intersite variation and allows sites to borrow strength from one another in a fully Bayesian framework. The advantage of training the models on the large independent data set, compared with just using the ADNI, is that the ADNI consists of many sites with small sample sizes. This would result in unstable estimates of normative distributions that could be strongly influenced by outliers or sampling bias. Here, by training on over n = 33,000 from only 9 data sets (with 60 sites), the model produces a stable distribution of estimates across the entire lifespan. Next, these estimates were conditioned to our specific context, using an adapted transfer learning approach. The parameters of the reference normative model were recalibrated to the ADNI data set using 70% of healthy controls per ADNI site, where 70% was used to give stable estimates of the transferred model parameters, given that many of the scan sites in the ADNI have quite small sample sizes. The remaining 30% of healthy controls plus MCI and patients with AD were used to assess the heterogeneity in neuroanatomical presentation.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear regression was used to test group differences in mean cortical thickness Z-score and total outlier count (tOC), adjusting for age and sex. Region-level group comparisons used χ² tests with FDR correction. Hamming distance was computed to measure dissimilarity between individuals' binary outlier patterns, with group comparisons using ANOVA. Linear regression adjusting for age, sex, years of education, and Clinical Dementia Rating (sum of boxes) examined relationships between tOC and cognitive composite scores (ADNI MEM for memory, ADNI EF for executive function); interactional effects of diagnostic group were assessed. Linear regression adjusting for age and sex examined relationships between tOC and CSF markers (Aβ and p-tau), with group interaction effects tested. Cox proportional hazards regression assessed whether tOC predicted MCI to AD conversion within 3 years, controlling for age and sex. Kaplan-Meier plots illustrated conversion risk stratified by median tOC split.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Patients with AD showed highly heterogeneous patterns of cortical thickness outliers (median 12 outlier regions), with greater within-group dissimilarity than MCI or controls; higher outlier counts were associated with worse cognitive function, CSF biomarkers (lower Aβ, higher p-tau), and increased risk of MCI to AD conversion (hazard ratio 1.028 per region).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Patients with AD (n=206) had a median of 12 outlier regions (out of 148), with the highest proportion of outliers (47%) in the parahippocampal gyrus. For 62 regions, over 90% of AD patients had cortical thickness within the normal range, demonstrating substantial heterogeneity. AD patients had significantly more outlier regions than MCI (n=662, median 4 outliers) or controls (n=159, median 2 outliers) (F(2,1022)=95.39, p=2.0×10⁻¹⁶). Patients with AD were also more dissimilar to each other than MCI or controls, as measured by Hamming distance (F(2,1024)=209.42, p=2.2×10⁻¹⁶), with AD showing median Hamming distance of 32 compared to 10 for MCI and 6 for controls. Greater numbers of outlier regions were significantly associated with worse memory performance (β=-0.01, p=2.2×10⁻¹⁶) and executive function (β=-0.02, p=2.2×10⁻¹⁶). Higher tOC was associated with lower CSF Aβ (β=0.002, p=0.022) and higher CSF p-tau (β=0.1301, p=1.04×10⁻⁸). In survival analysis of 454 MCI participants followed for up to 3 years, 76 converted to AD. For every 10-point increase in tOC, the risk of converting from MCI to AD increased by 31.4% (hazard ratio 1.028, 95% CI 1.016-1.039, p=1.8×10⁻¹⁶). Regional patterns showed outliers were most prevalent in temporoparietal regions, though substantial individual variation existed even among patients matched for age, sex, ApoE genotype, and MMSE scores.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Reference dataset may not be fully representative of healthy population; ADNI participants may not reflect general clinical population; reference data processed with mixed FreeSurfer versions (5 and 6) potentially adding noise to normative models; ADNI comprises mainly early-stage dementia, limiting insights into late-stage heterogeneity; underrepresentation of cognitive domains beyond memory and executive function; cross-sectional design limits understanding of temporal heterogeneity; only cortical thickness was examined (subcortical volumes not included); need for longitudinal data to map individual trajectories over time; visuospatial and other non-memory symptoms not extensively characterized; potential sampling bias from research volunteers.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The total outlier count (tOC) has potential as an individual patient metric of brain health to inform clinical decisions. The approach provides more individualized assessment compared to previous methods that used smaller normative samples, limited regional coverage, or did not account for site effects. Individual normative maps could potentially index disease progression or evaluate effectiveness of disease-modifying treatments tailored to individual patients. The methodology could be extended to include subcortical volumes using appropriate reference datasets. Future applications should incorporate longitudinal data and potentially combine with data-driven staging methods (e.g., SuStaIn) to account for disease stage while preserving individual-level heterogeneity information. The approach addresses limitations of subtyping methods which assume within-cluster homogeneity and may not capture individual-level variation, particularly important for atypical presentations.

general_notes.general_notes: This is the first application of neuroanatomical normative modeling to Alzheimer disease using hierarchical Bayesian regression. The study demonstrates that AD affects different individuals in heterogeneous ways, with marked variability in spatial patterns of cortical atrophy. The reference dataset combined data from 9 large-scale studies: detailed composition is in supplementary eTable 1 (including OASIS, ABCD, UK Biobank, and others across 60 sites total). The hierarchical Bayesian regression approach (as implemented in PCNtoolkit v0.20) was specifically chosen for its ability to handle multi-site data efficiently. The transfer learning adaptation using 70% of ADNI controls per site was necessary because many ADNI sites have small sample sizes. Case studies in the paper (Figure 4B) illustrated that even patients matched for age, sex, ApoE ε4 genotype, and MMSE scores can show markedly different spatial patterns of cortical thickness outliers. The paper was previously published as a preprint on medRxiv (doi: 10.1101/2022.06.30.22277053). Analysis code is available on GitHub (github.com/serenaverdi/ADNI_normative-modelling). ADNI data sharing follows ADNI Data Sharing and Publications Committee guidelines. The study received funding from EPSRC, NIH/ADNI, and various other sources. Article processing charge was funded by METAFORA Biosystems. This is an open access article (CC BY-NC-ND license).
